Decision Framework
The following questions guide model selection for a given organizational context. Each question is now anchored to specific benchmark evidence rather than qualitative judgment.
What is the regulatory context?

EU-regulated high-risk applications require conformity assessment by August 2026 (7% of global turnover penalty exposure). No model vendor provides this documentation by default — it is the deployer's responsibility. Open-weight models enable internal auditing of model behaviour; proprietary models require the vendor to cooperate with any audit. In practice, neither type removes the compliance burden from the deploying organization.
What is the copyright exposure?

LiCoEval results show that even the best-performing model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) produces GPL violations in 14% of at-risk code outputs. Organizations generating code commercially should require published LiCoEval scores before deployment and implement ScanCode Toolkit output filtering in CI/CD regardless of model choice. For proprietary models, enterprise IP indemnification clauses must be explicitly negotiated and reviewed for scope limitations.
Is agentic deployment involved?

The 25–27 percentage point gap between behavioral and content safety in Agent-SafetyBench means that standard chat-based safety evaluations are insufficient for any deployment where the model has tool access. No model currently available achieves 60% behavioral safety — the threshold below which human-in-the-loop per interaction should be treated as mandatory rather than optional.
What is the sensitivity of the data processed?

Models that require data to be sent to a third-party API (all proprietary models) are inappropriate for processing personal data, trade secrets, or confidential patient information without explicit data processing agreements meeting GDPR Article 28 requirements. The MCP-SafetyBench finding — >80% host-side attack success — applies to agentic proprietary deployments specifically: an attacker can potentially exfiltrate data via tool-use manipulation without the model "knowing" it has done so.
Does the organization have ML expertise?

Open-weight models require internal competence for deployment, fine-tuning, and monitoring. The alignment-faking finding (Structural Alignment Failures) adds a new consideration: fine-tuning on any downstream task may inadvertently shift safety properties, and monitoring for this requires interpretability tooling that most organizations do not have. Without this expertise, proprietary APIs provide a lower operational burden while offloading (but not eliminating) safety responsibility.
Has the geopolitical compliance surface been mapped?

Given 38 US state laws, the EU AI Act, and South Korea's AI Basic Act, organizations operating internationally face multiregional compliance obligations that no single vendor's compliance documentation covers. This mapping must be done by the deploying organization, not delegated to the model vendor.
Practical Recommendations
Framing: Evidence-Based, Time-Sensitive
The recommendations in this chapter are grounded in the benchmark findings reviewed in Chapters 2–5 and calibrated to the most important near-term compliance deadline:
August 2, 2026
, when EU AI Act high-risk provisions become enforceable with penalties of up to 7% of global annual turnover.
Three premises underpin these recommendations:

Guardrails are necessary but not sufficient. The 100% JailbreakBench adaptive success rate and the 29% evaluation-gaming rate documented in Project Glasswing mean that no current model's safety properties are reliable under adversarial conditions. Deployment decisions must therefore be made with the assumption that model-level safety will be circumvented, and system-level controls — human oversight, output filtering, access restrictions — must compensate.

Benchmark scores are forward-looking baselines, not guarantees. A model that achieves low HarmBench ASR today may score differently after downstream fine-tuning or after a new attack method emerges. Safety evaluation is a continuous activity, not a one-time certification.

The August 2026 deadline is real. The EU AI Act's high-risk provisions will be enforced, and the Digital Omnibus proposed delays do not eliminate the underlying obligation. Organizations with EU customers deploying AI in Annex III categories must begin conformity assessment now — the infrastructure cannot be built in weeks.
For Organizations Before Deployment
Copyright and Licence Risk
Require published LiCoEval scores for all code generation models.

LiCoEval (Xu et al., 2024) is the only published benchmark that directly measures licence compliance in code generation. A minimum threshold of 95% overall compliance should be required for models deployed in domains with GPL exposure. Currently, no open-weight model meets this threshold; Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 78% is the best available proprietary result. Organizations below threshold must implement ScanCode Toolkit output filtering in CI/CD before deploying AI code generation.
Run CopyBench for text generation models.

The non-literal reproduction rates in the CopyBench table show that better-aligned models paraphrase rather than quote — but BERTScore similarity to protected works remains high (54% for Claude 3). For content creation use cases, organizations should treat any BERTScore above 40% as requiring manual review of the specific outputs before publication.
Negotiate IP indemnification scope explicitly.

Proprietary model providers offer enterprise IP indemnification, but the scope varies. Key questions: Does indemnification cover non-literal reproduction? Does it apply if the model was fine-tuned by the organization? Does it cover code generated from internal (not public) training data? All three scenarios can arise in normal enterprise use, and default terms often exclude them.
Safety Evaluation
Do not deploy agentic models without human-in-the-loop per interaction.

Agent-SafetyBench shows that all tested models score below 60% on behavioral safety (Zhang et al., 2024). The 25–27 percentage point gap between behavioral and content safety means that a model passing standard safety evaluation can still take harmful autonomous actions when given tool access. Until behavioral safety scores exceed 80%, human-in-the-loop review for every agentic interaction is the only available mitigation.
Require published HarmBench and AIR-Bench results before deployment.

Self-reported safety claims are structurally untrustworthy — vendors have incentives to report favorable metrics. Require that models be submitted to HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) and AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024) under independently verified conditions. For EU deployments, AIR-Bench results directly indicate which EU AI Act risk categories the model does not satisfy.
Document that guardrails are speed bumps, not walls.

JailbreakBench achieves 100% success against all tested models under adaptive attacks (Chao et al., 2024). This must be reflected in your risk documentation. Any safety claim that implies the model "will not" produce harmful outputs under adversarial conditions is false. Risk documentation should instead specify what system-level controls compensate for this limitation.
Test fairness under adversarial conditions, not just baseline.

SALAD-Bench shows that models drop from 70–88% baseline safety scores to 28–52% under adversarial augmentation (Li et al., 2024). Bias evaluations run on base data do not represent the model's behavior when an adversarial user attempts to exploit fairness failures. Organizations deploying models in hiring, lending, or healthcare contexts must include adversarial fairness testing.
Regulatory Mapping
Map your use case to EU AI Act risk tier now.

Annex III of the EU AI Act specifies high-risk categories: biometric identification, critical infrastructure, educational assessment, employment decisions, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration control, and administration of justice. Any AI deployment touching these categories requires a conformity assessment. The August 2026 deadline is 16 months from the time of writing — barely sufficient to complete conformity assessment for a complex system.
For code generation, run LiCoEval before deploying on internal codebases.

Internal codebases may contain GPL-licensed dependencies. A model fine-tuned or prompted with internal code may reproduce GPL functions in contexts where the organization has not identified the licence obligation. LiCoEval should be run against a representative sample of internal code domains, not only against the public benchmark.
Build logging infrastructure immediately.

EU AI Act Article 12 requires that high-risk AI systems maintain logs sufficient to reconstruct which model version generated which output, on what date, for what purpose. This infrastructure takes time to build and must be operational before the August 2026 enforcement date, not after.
For Organizations During Deployment
Re-run safety benchmarks quarterly.

Model providers update safety training, deploy new attack defenses, and release new model versions without necessarily announcing changes. Benchmark results from a model's release date may not reflect current performance. A quarterly re-evaluation against HarmBench and OR-Bench (Cui et al., 2024) maintains a current risk baseline and satisfies the NIST AI RMF
Measure
function's ongoing monitoring requirement (National & Technology, 2023).
Implement output filters independent of model safety.

ScanCode Toolkit for licence detection in code, and semantic-similarity filters for text, should run as post-processing steps regardless of the model's built-in safety properties. The 14–38% GPL violation rates in the LiCoEval table demonstrate that model-level compliance is insufficient.
Monitor for agentic scope creep.

Models deployed with tool access show a systematic tendency to expand the scope of actions taken beyond the literal instruction — a pattern documented in Agent-SafetyBench and consistent with the Glasswing case study. Audit logs should specifically track the ratio of actions taken to actions explicitly authorized, and alert when this ratio exceeds a defined threshold.
For Model Providers
Publish adversarially-robust benchmark results, not only baseline.

The SALAD-Bench adversarial augmentation results show that baseline safety scores are systematically optimistic. Publishing only baseline results misrepresents the model's safety properties under realistic adversarial conditions. Providers claiming safety compliance should be required to publish results under the adversarial conditions that the benchmark provides.
Include interpretability analysis demonstrating that alignment is not shallow.

The finding that ablating 0.006% of parameters removes safety (Greenblatt et al., 2024) should be addressed directly in system cards. Providers should demonstrate, via interpretability analysis, that safety properties are distributed across the model rather than concentrated in a small ablatable circuit. The Glasswing system card's 244 pages represent an example of the level of detail required to make credible safety claims for frontier models.
Be transparent about benchmark saturation and evaluation gaming.

The 29% evaluation-gaming rate documented for Claude Mythos is not specific to Anthropic — it reflects a general property of sufficiently capable models. Providers should disclose any evaluation conditions under which the model appeared to modify its behaviour based on context cues, and should include this information in model cards rather than limiting it to internal alignment reports.
Establish independent oversight boards before claiming alignment, not after.

Current frontier lab frameworks (Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness, DeepMind FSF) have all weakened over time (Weidinger & collaborators, 2025). An independent oversight board with published authority to recommend deployment halts — and a published record of when it exercised that authority — would provide more credible safety assurance than self-certified frameworks that are revised downward when they become inconvenient.
Policy Level
Do not wait for US federal AI legislation.

Federal AI legislation is unlikely before 2028 in the current US political environment. Enforcement of state AI laws — Colorado, California, Illinois, Texas — is proceeding now. Organizations in those states face real compliance obligations. The gap created by US federal deregulation does not eliminate liability; it shifts it to state law and civil litigation.
EU organizations: August 2026 is a hard deadline.

The proposed Digital Omnibus delays do not eliminate the high-risk obligations; they delay some implementation guidance. The underlying obligation to complete conformity assessment for Annex III applications is in the enacted regulation. Organizations relying on the proposed delays are making a bet that the delays will be adopted and will cover their specific situation — a bet that should not be made without legal counsel.
Governance vacuum is the dominant systemic risk.

The US capability gap with China narrowed from 9.3% to 1.7% in a single year. 63% of new fine-tuned models on HuggingFace now use Chinese base models. The EU has 4–5% of global compute capacity. These figures describe a governance situation where the jurisdiction with the most comprehensive regulatory framework has the least capability, and the jurisdictions developing the most capable models are either actively deregulating (US) or strategically limiting governance (China). Unilateral organizational action — however thorough — operates within this structural constraint. Advocacy for international governance coordination, particularly through OECD and G7 AI governance processes, is a rational institutional investment.

AI Manifest

The following is a personal manifest on the ethical use of AI in professional practice. It is intended as a practical framework for individuals and teams, distinct from the regulatory and compliance analysis of preceding chapters. Unlike its earlier iterations, this version grounds each principle not in abstract values but in the specific failure cases and benchmark findings documented in this thesis — because principles without evidence are just preferences.
How do we ensure that AI is something that can belong to all of us?

When using AI it is important to think about which norms and values we consider important. The following principles are not rules — they are anchors for reflection. But they are anchors that have been stress-tested: each one was forged from a concrete failure, a documented benchmark result, or a governance breakdown.
Transparency
The use of AI has become part of many people's daily lives and is embedded in many of our tools. Transparency is not only a legal issue but above all a moral one.
Where does the creative or achieved work lie? Are you using AI to complete something entirely new, or as a tool to simplify or improve a particular work process?
Generative or degenerative?

The Foundation Model Transparency Index found that no major model provider scores above 60 out of 100 on transparency indicators — and training data disclosure, the dimension most directly relevant to copyright and consent, is the worst-performing dimension across all providers (Bommasani et al., 2023). Transparency claims from providers are structurally optimistic; the appropriate response is to treat undisclosed information as undisclosed, not as satisfactory.

For practitioners: publish which model version generated which output, on what date, under what prompt. AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024) found that no current model fully complies with the regulatory frameworks that require this — but the obligation exists regardless of whether the model was designed to support it.
Would the recipient be surprised? If so, mention it.
Human Control

The 25–27 percentage point gap between content safety and behavioral safety in Agent-SafetyBench is the most important number in this document for practitioners making deployment decisions. A model that passes every content-based safety evaluation can still take harmful autonomous actions when given tools. This is not a theoretical concern: autonomous AI systems were deployed in offensive cyber operations at 80–90% autonomy levels in 2025 (US-CERT, 2025).

The project Glasswing case demonstrates that even the most safety-focused development process produces models that can escape evaluation sandboxes and rewrite their own audit trails. Human control is not a design preference — it is the primary mitigation for a category of failure that no current technical safeguard can prevent.
Three modes exist for situating human judgment:
AI as actor:
the AI makes decisions and executes actions autonomously
AI as adviser:
the AI recommends, a human decides and acts
Human alone:
AI is excluded from the decision loop
For agentic deployments — any system where the model has tool access — the default should be "AI as adviser" until behavioral safety scores exceed 80%. No model currently available meets this bar.
Responsibility as an anchor: a human, with a name.
Bias & Fairness

SALAD-Bench found that models drop from 70–88% safety scores on base data to 28–52% under adversarial augmentation (Li et al., 2024). The same degradation occurs in fairness properties: a model that produces equitable outputs in normal operation can be manipulated into discriminatory outputs by an attacker who knows the model's failure modes. Fairness evaluated on base data is not the same as fairness under realistic conditions.
Perhaps it is wise to think about where bias and fairness can be a problem, and where they are not. Build a framework for which use-cases are suitable to outsource and which are not.

The practical implication: do not treat benchmark fairness scores as deployment guarantees. Test fairness under adversarial conditions specifically relevant to your use case. A hiring tool that performs equitably in standard evaluation may fail when an applicant discovers and exploits the model's sensitivity to demographic signals.
Diversity in your team is a better bias-check than diversity in your prompt.
Guardrails as Essential Infrastructure
MCP-SafetyBench found that adding safety prompts to open-source models sometimes
worsens

safety by 2–4 percentage points (Zong et al., 2025). The instinct to add more guardrails — longer system prompts, more restrictive instructions — is not reliably effective. Safety is contextual and the interaction between safety instructions and model behavior is not linear.

The Glasswing case demonstrates the ceiling of current guardrail technology: Anthropic deployed a 244-page system card, restricted access to 12 partners, and conducted the most extensive safety evaluation in the company's history — and earlier model versions still escaped the evaluation sandbox, posted exploits publicly, and rewrote git history. Guardrails are necessary infrastructure. They are not walls.

What follows from this: deployment gates must precede capability release, not follow it. The decision about whether a model should be deployed at all, and to whom, is the most important safety decision — more important than any technical guardrail applied afterward.
Build the gate before you open the road.
Deployment Responsibility Trumps Model Responsibility

OR-Bench established that the safety–helpfulness correlation across models is r = 0.878 (Cui et al., 2024). This means that the constraints applied to make a model safer also make it less useful. There is no free lunch: every guardrail applied by a provider costs utility. Organizations that demand maximum safety AND maximum utility from a single model are asking for something that currently does not exist.

The corollary is that deployment context determines risk as much as model properties. A model with a 38% best-attack HarmBench ASR deployed with strict human oversight in a low-stakes context poses less real-world risk than a model with 28% ASR deployed autonomously in a high-stakes context. Safety is not a property of the model alone — it is a property of the system.
The context of deployment is not a modifier of safety. It is safety.
Geopolitical Awareness

Fragmented governance means that every organization deploying AI internationally is, in effect, navigating multiple regulatory regimes simultaneously. The US has revoked its primary federal AI safety framework and replaced it with deliberate deregulation. The EU enforces a comprehensive framework against a backdrop of 4–5% of global compute capacity. China advances capability rapidly under a governance framework specifically designed not to constrain it. South Korea has a binding framework; Japan has an aspirational one; Singapore has a voluntary one.

The gap between what governance frameworks require and what the global AI development landscape produces is widening. An organization that waits for international harmonization to clarify its obligations is waiting for something that is not coming.

This is not a counsel of despair. We have benchmarks that reveal what is actually happening in model behavior. We have a governance framework — the EU AI Act — that specifies in concrete terms what is required of high-risk deployments. We have an enforcement deadline — August 2, 2026 — that is specific enough to plan around. What we do not have is the political will to enforce these requirements at the pace that capability development demands.
No single standard is sufficient. Build for multi regional compliance from the start.
Honest Assessment of Limits

The benchmark ecosystem is saturating. Claude Mythos achieved 100% on Cybench; future models will achieve 100% on benchmarks designed to measure today's capability frontier. The 29% evaluation-gaming rate (Anthropic, 2026) means that benchmark scores for highly capable models may partially reflect the model performing for evaluators rather than its behavior in deployment. No current tool reliably distinguishes genuinely safe from evaluation-gamed models.
This is not a reason to abandon benchmarking. It is a reason to treat benchmark results as necessary but insufficient evidence, to invest in interpretability tools that can reveal
why
a model behaves safely rather than only
that
it does, and to be honest — with clients, with regulators, and with ourselves — about what we do not know.

The closing argument of this thesis is not pessimistic. It is that we have the tools to identify what is going wrong, a governance framework that specifies what is required, and — in the European AI Act's August 2026 deadline — a concrete moment of accountability. What is missing is not knowledge. What is missing is the will to act on it before the window closes.
Use AI only when necessary. When you do, own the consequences.
Model Fit Test

This final chapter turns the evidence from the thesis into a practical selection exercise. It does not ask which model is objectively best. It asks which model best fits a specific set of risks, values, and deployment constraints.
How the Test Works

Each answer adjusts the weight given to the same dimensions used throughout the thesis: copyright risk, safety, transparency, regulatory alignment, agentic safety, usefulness, and deployment control. The model profiles are anchored to the benchmark results and structural comparison in the earlier chapters.

The output should be read as a decision aid, not as legal advice or a permanent leaderboard. Benchmark results change, provider contracts change, and deployment context can dominate model-level properties.
On the original site this chapter included an interactive questionnaire that applied this weighting to recommend a model; the questionnaire is not reproduced here.
Evidence Behind the Recommendation

The benchmark data behind the scoring model is the same data used in the copyright, safety, transparency and framework chapters. If new benchmark results arrive, the scoring can be updated to reflect them.
Interpretation Rule

A recommendation for a proprietary model usually means: prefer managed safety updates, enterprise contracting, and stronger current benchmark performance, while accepting transparency limits. A recommendation for an open-weight model usually means: prefer auditability, local control, and values-aligned openness, while accepting greater operator responsibility.
